Url.Title: Backup Bundle
Url.Abstract: Backup Bundle Backed-up CMS configurations are stored in "backup bundles", each of which is a gzipped tar file. When the backup action is invoked, a backup bundle is created and written to "/var/www/html/backup", using a user-specified file name. If a backup bundle already exists when the backup action is invoked, the existing file will be removed before the new bundle is created. The latest backup bundle will always remain until the next backup is made. After the backup has been created, the backup bundle is available for retrieval using HTTP GET.

Url.Title: Customer glossary definition
Url.Abstract: Customer Each server group must have a customer name as part of its definition. There is a built-in customer named DEFAULT, so it is not necessary to define a new customer if you do not have multiple customers using your site. Although it is necessary to have a customer as part of each server group definition, customers are not binding in any other respect, nor do they contribute to any other definition. There are Rank and Status parameters associated with customers, but these are provided for use at the user's discretion. The Rank and Status parameters provide another means for customers to be sorted, but they do not contribute to the definition of any other aspects of the configuration.

Url.Title: Introduction
Url.Abstract: Introduction This document describes methods and operations of how an external Security Information and Event Management System (SIEM) can receive security events and operational data from the SmartWall Corero Management Server (CMS) in a Syslog format. Corero is open to discussions with partners who are interested in receiving events through both mechanisms for a tighter integration.

Url.Title: Protection Groups and Clusters
Url.Abstract: Protection Groups and Clusters A protection group is the unit of protection and security services unit for a single 10Gbps link. A cluster comprises one or two protection groups, depending on whether the cluster is configured for HA redundancy or not.

Url.Title: Common Types and Formats
Url.Abstract: Common Types and Formats All messages and values within the security data content of a syslog message have consistent formatting across similar information content and information structure (e.g. the representation of tabular information). By understanding some of the common representations as they are made visible in the receiving tools, most of the messages are relatively self-describing. This section provides a description of these common representations.

Url.Title: Syslog Messages
Url.Abstract: Syslog Messages This section defines the contents of each syslog message generated by the CMS by category

Url.Title: Security Category
Url.Abstract: Security Category Block Rate Statistics Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that summarizes rate of packet blocking in the system for each of the overall classifications for security rules on the Defense appliances. There are several hundred security rules that may be protecting a specific network, and these rules are categorized into 8 categories so that the block rate per classification can be calculated. These classifications are provided below.

Url.Title: Top Security Rules Type
Url.Abstract: Top Security Rules Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that contains the security rules that had the highest blocked packet rates over the time period. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the rule that fired and the percentage of the samples. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: IP Address Classifications Type
Url.Abstract: IP Address Classifications Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that summarizes the classification of the IP addresses known across the Defense appliances. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Rule Statistics Type
Url.Abstract: Rule Statistics Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates one message for each active security rule in the system that contains the counts of the number of packets blocked or just detected and the number of security events issued for these two situations for that rule. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Threat Awareness Type
Url.Abstract: Threat Awareness Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that summarizes threat awareness status for a set of significant internal indicators across the Defense appliances. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Network Category
Url.Abstract: Network Category Interface Statistics Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that summarizes interface statistics for the external (from the Internet) and internal (toward the firewall and servers) ports of the protection groups on the Defense appliances. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Destination IP Addresses Type
Url.Abstract: Top Destination IP Addresses Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen destination IP addresses over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the IP address and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Source Ports Type
Url.Abstract: Top Source Ports Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen source IP ports over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the IP port and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Destination Ports Type
Url.Abstract: Top Destination Ports Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen destination IP ports over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the port and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Time-to-Live (ttl) Type
Url.Abstract: Top Time-to-Live (ttl) Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen Time-to-Live (ttl) fields over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the ttl and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Packet Length Type
Url.Abstract: Top Packet Length Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen specific packets lengths fields over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the length and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Usage Statistics Type
Url.Abstract: Usage Statistics Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that summarizes usage statistics on the Defense appliances. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Setup Rate Statistics Type
Url.Abstract: Setup Rate Statistics Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a report that summarizes setup rate statistics for flows on the Defense appliances. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Sflow Event Type
Url.Abstract: Sflow Event Type Each Network Threat Defense appliance samples the data stream and sends the samples to the CMS for threat and operational analysis. A subset of these events are sampled as well and sent as syslog messages for further integration in the SIEM analysis stream. Five messages per second are forwarded as syslog events.

Url.Title: System Category
Url.Abstract: System Category The system category contains messages that indicate the operational health of the Corero appliances and CMS.

Url.Title: Alarm Type
Url.Abstract: Alarm Type The CMS generates alarms for significant system events. A single type of syslog message carries the information for each alarm. These alarms have fields that can be broken out and indexed, and they also carry the full text.

Url.Title: Additional Integration Options

Url.Title: IP Address Spoofing
Url.Abstract: IP Address Spoofing IP address spoofing is the technique of falsifying a packet's source IP address. This practice is useful first because it helps to conceal the origin of an attack by making it appear as though the packets are sent from one or more different hosts than they really are. Secondly, and possibly more importantly,spoofing can be used in reflection attacks and amplification attacks to make that falsified source address the target of attack traffic. Spoofing is used also in SYN flood attacks as a means of ensuring that connection requests are not completed.

Url.Title: Amplification Attack
Url.Abstract: Amplification Attack An amplification attack is one in which an attacker abuses a protocol's designed behavior so that the attacker can use a comparatively small amount of initiating traffic to direct a massive amount of attack traffic at the target. Two common examples of amplification attack are DNS amplification attacks and NTP amplification attacks. These attacks exploit the behavior of DNS and NTP to multiply the volume of initiating attack traffic possibly many, many times, depending on exactly how the initiating traffic is crafted. In addition, these attacks often employ botnets to make the volume of attack traffic even larger.

Url.Title: Application Attack
Url.Abstract: Application Attack An application attack exploits behavior at layer 7 of the OSI model to focus an attack narrowly on a very specific target, such as a web server or similar Internet-based service, without necessarily denying users access to other resources on that host.

Url.Title: DNS Flood Attack
Url.Abstract: DNS Flood Attack Definition This attack directs a massive number of DNS requests at a DNS server in an effort to consume its processing power or memory. Typically, the attacking packets are directed at port 53 on the target, the well-known UDP port usually associated with DNS. This attack should not be confused with the DNS amplification attack, which uses a comparatively small number of initiating packets with spoofed IP addresses to generate a massive amount of bandwidth-consuming traffic.Rather, this attack seeks to exhaust memory or processing power. These attacks may leverage the resources of service providers, especially those that don't place a lot of emphasis on the security of their outbound traffic, rather than their inbound traffic.

Url.Title: HTTP GET Flood Attack
Url.Abstract: HTTP Flood Attacks: GET and POST Definition These are volumetric attacks using massive numbers of either HTTP GET requests or HTTP POST instructions. Typically, these are simple, straightforward attacks that overwhelm the target with the sheer volume of their requests.

Url.Title: ICMP Flood Attack
Url.Abstract: ICMP Flood Attack Definition An ICMP flood attack is a volumetric attack, a flood of ICMP requests intended to overwhelm the target's ability to respond. The ICMP flood is simply a barrage of ICMP messages (frequently, echo requests, or ping) sent at such volume and speed that the server is unable to keep up with the requests. In addition, since the ICMP messages expect a response, bandwidth is consumed on the way out, as well, as the server responds to each of the huge number of requests with a response of its own. The end result is that the server's bandwidth is fully consumed, leaving no room for legitimate traffic.

Url.Title: Invalid Payload Packet Attack

Url.Title: IP Fragmentation Attack
Url.Abstract: IP Fragmentation Attack Definition This is a catch-all term for a variety of different attacks that exploit the otherwise legitimate behavior of segmenting large IP packets across multiple data link layer frames. These exploits include fragments that overlap, that are malformed, that are incomplete, too large, or too small. In many cases, the higher level protocol's attempt to re-assemble what it perceives to be the original packet from the faulty fragments results in a packet that is invalid or otherwise unusable, in turn causing a processing delay or a memory problem. Multiplied across a very large number of such faulty fragments and invalid packets, the end result is the denial of service to legitimate users.

Url.Title: IP Option Exploit
Url.Abstract: Crafted IP Option Attack Definition A.k.a., the "Christmas tree" attack. In this attack, IP packets sent to the target have all of their possible options set, including combinations that are invalid. Used singly or in small numbers, these packets are useful as probes, as they can be used to determine what services reside on which interfaces at the target. Used in large numbers, these packets constitute a denial of service attack, as it takes the target a considerable amount of time to sort through all the options specified in each packet.

Url.Title: LAND Attack
Url.Abstract: LAND Attack Definition LAND is an acronym for "local area network denial." In this attack, the attacker sends packets to the target that have that target's IP address and port specified as both the source address and the destination address, causing the target to respond to itself endlessly. The attack sends these packets in large volume, resulting in denial of service to legitimate users.

Url.Title: Out of Sequence Attack
Url.Abstract: Out of Sequence Attack Definition The TCP out of sequence attack exploits TCP's connection-oriented behavior to deny service to legitimate users. One of TCP's features is that it handles data in the order that it is sent, which, under ordinary, legitimate circumstances, means that the data reaches the user in a sequential, understandable manner (think of simple examples such as a web page, an Email message, or a video segment). When TCP receives packets that are not in the correct order, it holds onto them until it has received them all and can arrange them in the correct sequence before providing them to the user. In addition, TCP does not limit the number of packets that can be buffered until they can be assembled sequentially; rather, this is a function of the target's memory. An attacker can abuse this feature by intentionally sending a very large number of TCP packets out of sequence, filling the target's memory, and therefore denying access to legitimate users.

Url.Abstract: Slowloris Attack Definition Slowloris is an attack aimed specifically at web servers, and is focused so tightly that it will leave other services running on the same host untouched. Slowloris works by initiating connections to the target and sending incomplete HTTP requests very slowly, thus consuming available connections and keeping them occupied as they wait for HTTP requests that never complete.

Url.Title: Smurf Attack
Url.Abstract: Smurf Attack Definition A Smurf attack is a variant of ICMP flood attack that uses the technique of amplification. Unlike a traditional ICMP flood attack, which simply bombards its target directly with ICMP packets, a Smurf attack broadcasts a very large number of ICMP requests to an available network. The source address of those ICMP packets, though, has been prepared (spoofed) with the IP address of the intended target. When the hosts to which the requests have been broadcast respond to those ICMP requests, they respond to the source IP address contained in the packet, which is that of the target. Subsequently, the target is inundated with ICMP responses, consuming its bandwidth and making it unavailable to legitimate users.

Url.Title: Sockstress Attack
Url.Abstract: Sockstress Attack Definition Sockstress attacks are a type of attack that directs unusual traffic at a target's available TCP connections, with the intention of consuming them and preventing legitimate users from reaching them. Typically, these attacks complete the TCP three-way handshake, and exploit some subsequent aspect of TCP's behavior to tie up the connection.

Url.Title: SYN Flood Attack
Url.Abstract: SYN Flood Attack Definition A SYN flood attack is a volumetric attack, a flood of TCP SYN requests directed at a target with the intent of consuming all of its available TCP connections, leaving none available for legitimate traffic. This common attack abuses the design of TCP's three-way handshake for establishing a valid connection between a client and a server.

Url.Title: TCP No Flag Attack
Url.Abstract: TCP No Flag Attack Definition A.k.a., a TCP null packet. This attack uses TCP packets with no flag set (no SYN, ACK, or RST), which makes the packet invalid. These packets are useful probes for identifying open ports on a target., and they may be used in combination with one or more other types of attack during a denial of service attack.

Url.Title: TCP SYN+FIN Attack
Url.Abstract: TCP SYN+FIN Attack Definition This attack involves sending a TCP packet that has both the SYN flag and the FIN flag set. Though the response can vary somewhat, the target typically responds to both flags, first acknowledging the SYN and transitioning to SYN_RCVD, then acknowledging the FIN, and transitioning to CLOSE_WAIT, where it stays stuck until the keep-alive value expires. Multiplied by a large number of such malicious packets, this results in an inability to respond to legitimate traffic, and a corresponding denial of service.

Url.Title: TCP SYN Fragment Attack
Url.Abstract: TCP SYN Fragment Attack Definition The TCP SYN fragment attack is a variation on the SYN flood attack that uses incomplete TCP SYN messages. In this attack, the target is inundated with incomplete TCP SYN messages, which it collects and holds onto while it waits for the rest of the message to re-assemble the corresponding packet. In actuality, the rest of the message is never sent, the packet never gets re-assembled, and the target's memory buffer fills up with incomplete SYN fragments, resulting in an inability for legitimate traffic to connect.

Url.Title: TCP Zero Window Attack
Url.Abstract: TCP Zero Window Attack Definition The TCP receive window size is a buffer that controls the amount of data that a TCP connection can accept and prepare for processing. In this attack, the attacker sends TCP packets with the TCP window size intentionally set to 0, rendering the connection unable to accept data.

Url.Title: Teardrop Attack
Url.Abstract: Teardrop Attack Definition The teardrop attack is a type of IP fragmentation attack, combining overlapping packet fragments with excessively large payloads. If the target succeeds in re-assembling the overlapping fragments, it encounters an invalid and unmanageably large packet.

Url.Title: UDP Flood Attack
Url.Abstract: UDP Flood Attack Definition A UDP flood attack is a volumetric attack, a flood of UDP packets. Typically, a UDP attack consists of a huge number of packets directed at randomly selected ports on the target server. The target responds by checking to see what applications it might have listening on those ports, and, if no application is listening there, the server responds with an ICMP Destination Unreachable message. The huge number of inbound requests combined with the similarly huge number of responses traveling outbound consumes the server's bandwidth, making it unreachable by legitimate users.

Url.Title: Volumetric Attacks
Url.Abstract: Volumetric Attack A volumetric attack is one that seeks to overwhelm its target by consuming all of one or more of its available resources, such as bandwidth or memory. In a volumetric attack, the attacker directs so much illegitimate traffic at the target that traffic from legitimate users is starved of the targeted resource.and denied altogether. TCP SYN floods, ICMP floods, and UDP floods are common examples of volumetric attacks.

Url.Abstract: Security Event Type Security events are generated by the Defense Appliances as they provide the security of the system. Security event information is sent from the appliances to the controlling CMS where they are locally processed and analyzed to provide Corero customers with immediate security state and attack information. In parallel with this local analysis, security events are sent to configured SIEMs for historical storage and additional processing.

Url.Title: System State Change Type
Url.Abstract: System State Change Type When certain significant system or network events occur, the CMS will issue a message indicating this change of state. The following is an example how this report is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Reflection Flood Signature Type
Url.Abstract: Top Reflection Flood Signature Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently signatures for potential reflection attacks over the time period as determined by each Network Threat Defense appliance inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the signature and its rates. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Server Groups Type
Url.Abstract: Top Server Groups Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen destination server groups over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. Server groups are configured in the CMS in the context of server protection instances. This configuration includes lists of IP addresses, ranges, and networks that are to receive the specific protection defined in that configuration. This statistic aggregates the destination IP addresses of the sampled packets into the configured server groups and determines the rank ordering of these server groups for each time period.

Url.Title: Top Service Flood Signature Type
Url.Abstract: Top Service Flood Signature Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently signatures for potential service protocol flood attacks over the time period as determined by each Network Threat Defense appliance inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the signature and its rates. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Source IP Addresses Type
Url.Abstract: Top Source IP Addresses Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen source IP addresses over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the IP address and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.

Url.Title: Top Source IP Subnets Type
Url.Abstract: Top Source IP Subnets Type Every 60 seconds the CMS creates a message that contains the most frequently seen IP subnets for the source IPs over the time period as determined by sflow sampling of the data inbound from the Internet into the site. Because the subnet is not contained in the IP packet, IPv4 /24 subnet and IPv6 /56 subnets are assumed. There will be up to 10 entries in each message and each one contains the subnet and its percent of the samples. The following is an example how this message is sent to configured syslog receivers and a description of the contents.
